eduassets.title: eduAssets
eduassets.description: Full stack system in use at a public school in São Paulo state: it tracks 192 devices, has handled over 66 tickets, and generates the reports used every week to declare inventory to state inspectors. TypeScript and Vite frontend, Node.js API with Express 5, Prisma and PostgreSQL, and optional RFID reading.

intro: eduAssets is a school equipment management system I built while working at PROATI to digitize the control of loans, returns and incidents. It now tracks all 192 devices at a public school in Pindamonhangaba and has handled over 66 tickets.

sections.heading: The Problem
paragraphs: School environments often rely on spreadsheets or manual logs to track IT equipment — laptops, projectors, tablets. This leads to lost assets, unclear responsibility, and time-consuming audits.
I wanted to build something that actually solved this, not just demonstrate CRUD operations.

sections.heading: Real-World Use
paragraphs: The reports generated by the system are used every week to declare inventory to inspectors and agents of the State of São Paulo. The project runs in production and is maintained with frequent deployments through CI/CD.

sections.heading: Architecture
paragraphs: The frontend is feature-first: each feature (assets, loans, users) has its own directory with its components, services, and types. The API uses Express 5 with Prisma as the ORM and Zod for runtime validation, deployed on an Oracle Cloud VPS behind Nginx in a Docker container.

sections.heading: Access and Security
paragraphs: The API is the security boundary. Access is split into Guest (read-only), Editor and Administrator roles, with write permissions enforced on the backend. In the browser, sessions use HttpOnly cookies only, and state-changing requests require a trusted Origin.

sections.heading: What I Learned
paragraphs: This project taught me to plan an architecture before writing code. Making early decisions — like the feature-first structure and the clear separation between frontend and API — prevented costly refactors throughout development.

buenos-aires-explorer.title: Buenos Aires Explorer
buenos-aires-explorer.description: Desktop application in C# and .NET 10 for registering points of interest in Buenos Aires and building visit itineraries. It looks up coordinates and addresses through the Nominatim API and images on Wikimedia, calculates distances between stops with the Haversine formula, shows the itinerary on an interactive map and exports it to PDF. Version 1.0.0 is published, with a ready-to-download executable.

intro: Buenos Aires Explorer is a desktop application in C# and Windows Forms for registering points of interest in Buenos Aires and planning visit itineraries, with an interactive map, distance calculation and PDF export. Version 1.0.0 is published, with a ready-to-download executable.

sections.heading: The Challenge
paragraphs: The goal was to explore desktop development with C# and Windows Forms, focusing on clean architecture, a custom interface and integration with external services, bringing location management, itineraries and map visualization into a single application.

sections.heading: Technical Highlights
paragraphs: The code is organized in layers (Models, Services, Views, UI and Data), with Entity Framework Core and SQLite for persistence and migrations. It comes to about 6,900 lines of C#.
The interface uses 7 custom visual components built on Windows Forms, such as RoundedButton and RoundedDateTimePicker, plus a custom theme with per-category colors.
The Nominatim API handles forward and reverse geocoding, and Wikimedia provides location images, searching by coordinates with a fallback to the title.

In itineraries, the user sets the order of the stops, and the application calculates per-leg and total distances with the Haversine formula. The interactive map uses Leaflet.js through WebView2, and itineraries can be exported to PDF with QuestPDF.

dev-portfolio.title: Developer Portfolio
dev-portfolio.description: Rebuilt from a hand-written vanilla JavaScript site into React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS on React Router, with every page pre-rendered to static HTML in three languages. Per-page SEO metadata, a hash-based Content-Security-Policy, flash-free dark and high-contrast themes, and end-to-end tests with automated accessibility checks.

intro: This portfolio began as a hand-written vanilla JavaScript site. It was migrated in planned, tested phases to React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS — keeping the same design while turning every project into a real page with its own address, share preview and search metadata.

sections.heading: Architecture
paragraphs: React Router runs in framework mode with server rendering turned off: every page — the home page and each project, in English, Portuguese and Spanish — is pre-rendered to static HTML at build time and then hydrated in the browser. There is no runtime server to maintain.
The code is organized by responsibility (app, pages, widgets, features, entities, shared), and a test fails the build if a lower layer imports a higher one.

sections.heading: Languages and SEO
paragraphs: The language is part of the URL (/, /pt, /es). Each page has its own title, description, canonical address, hreflang alternates, social preview and structured data, and the sitemap is generated from the same route data.
All copy lives in typed JSON files: a misspelled key fails the type check, and tests make sure the three languages always share the same structure.

sections.heading: Security, accessibility and performance
paragraphs: A Content-Security-Policy is generated for every page with a hash of each inline script, so no inline code runs unless it was built into the page. A tiny script in the document head applies the saved theme and language before the first paint — no flash of the wrong theme.

Animations respect the reduced-motion setting and load only when the browser is idle; a first visit downloads about 140 kB of JavaScript. A Playwright suite covers routing, languages, themes, the contact form and automated accessibility checks.

aviation-safety.title: Aviation Safety Project
aviation-safety.description: Built a Python data pipeline using Pandas for transformation and normalization of simulated aeronautical incident records, exported via OpenPyXL, and visualized in Power BI.

intro: A Python data pipeline that processes simulated aeronautical incident records, applies transformations and normalizations with Pandas, exports results via OpenPyXL, and generates visualizations in Power BI.

sections.heading: The Pipeline
paragraphs: I deliberately separated the data generation, processing, and presentation stages into distinct layers. Each pipeline stage is independent — making each part easier to test, maintain, and evolve.

sections.heading: Visualizations
paragraphs: The processed data feeds a Power BI dashboard with metrics on the frequency, type, and severity of simulated incidents. The goal was to practice communicating data clearly to a non-technical audience.

parkschool-alpr.title: Parkschool ALPR
parkschool-alpr.alt: Sample Mercosur license plate highlighted by a detection frame
parkschool-alpr.description: Python microservice for automatic license plate recognition in a parking system. It processes camera frames, detects the plate, runs OCR, validates the Mercosur and legacy Brazilian formats, removes repeated readings and sends the event to the backend with retries and idempotency.

intro: Parkschool ALPR (Automatic License Plate Recognition) is the computer vision microservice of a parking control system, developed in the SENAC Capstone Project. It reads frames from a file, RTSP or USB camera, detects the plate, reads the characters and sends the event to a Node.js backend maintained by another team.

sections.heading: Architecture
paragraphs: The detector and reader sit behind interfaces, so the real models can be swapped for simulated versions in tests, with no camera or TensorFlow. A FastAPI service exposes /health/live and /health/ready, with counters for frames, events sent, duplicates and invalid readings.

sections.heading: Reliability
paragraphs: Each event has its own identifier, so retries do not create duplicate records. The HTTP client retries with exponential backoff on network failures and honors Retry-After. Only plates in the Mercosur and legacy formats are sent, without correcting ambiguous characters, and logs do not expose credentials or the full plate.

sections.heading: Models and Current Status
paragraphs: Detection and OCR use TensorFlow/Keras models, with training and evaluation scripts for the RodoSol-ALPR dataset and a model card that records each model's version, hash and metrics. Final training and measurement with real images are the next step, so the default mode still uses a simulated detector and OCR. The suite has more than 100 automated tests.
